findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is and what makes it different. They can say what it is within seconds.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says why it exists: to prove that Athena can explain an unfamiliar project with traceable sources. The claim ids and source links back this up, so a reader can check it.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The intro describes Athena as a tool that changes code, but the page shows a read-only study. It never says which command or request produced the study. A newcomer cannot connect the demo to the product, or reproduce it.
findings.source: "turns a short request into a change to a code repository" vs. "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The intro promises a second model that checks the work and per-step costs, but neither appears anywhere on the page. A newcomer sees no evidence of either feature.
findings.source: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost"

findings.text: What to do next is concrete and easy to find, and the header links to it. The page does not mention requirements such as model access or API keys, so a newcomer may run into problems that nothing here warns about.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" / "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Most of the page covers firstmate's internals: exit codes, lock behavior, capacity slots. A newcomer to Athena has to scroll past all of it, and there is little about Athena itself after the header.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (t1–t11), "Claims and sources" (c1–c44)

findings.text: Defining terms before using them helps, but the same definitions appear twice, almost word for word. The "in scope" entry admits "this page gives no test for it," which leaves a defined term empty.
findings.source: "Words used first" and Glossary entries for captain, yolo, in scope, green, red

findings.text: Some transition cards need a long aside to explain why a move goes nowhere, and a first-time reader will find them hard going. The cards are precise, but the page is aimed at a reader who already knows firstmate rather than at a newcomer.
findings.source: t10 "ready → ready": "The task stays Ready because merging does not end it: it is Done only when teardown later returns the worktree..."

findings.text: The page is open about its limits, which builds trust. It also tells the reader that nothing on the page was run or confirmed by running it.
findings.source: Limits of this study: "This study read the pinned tree only... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
